questions.question: What is a heading mainly designed to do?
choices: Signal the subject or organization of a section
Prove every claim in the section
Replace the main text
Identify the author's credentials

questions.question: How does a caption usually help a reader?
choices: It lists every source in the book
It explains or adds context to an image or graphic
It defines the text's central argument
It gives the page number

questions.question: A graph compares monthly rainfall across five cities. What can the graph communicate more efficiently than a paragraph?
choices: The cause of every rainfall change
The author's personal opinion
Patterns and differences in the data
A complete account of each city's history

questions.question: A bold word appears with a definition in the margin. What is the feature's purpose?
choices: Show that the word is a proper noun
Indicate that the text is fiction
Identify a quotation
Draw attention to a key term and clarify its meaning

questions.question: Which feature would best help a reader find the page where 'photosynthesis' is discussed?
choices: Index
Caption
Table of contents
Glossary

questions.question: A map includes a legend explaining colors and symbols. Why is the legend important?
choices: It proves the map is current
It explains how to interpret the map's visual information
It states the author's purpose
It replaces the scale

questions.question: A sidebar presents a short biography related to the main topic. How should a reader use it?
choices: As evidence that the main text is always biased
As a replacement for the central explanation
As supporting context that may deepen understanding of the main text
As the book's index

questions.question: A table lists experimental results in rows and columns. What is a useful first step?
choices: Assume the largest number is the conclusion
Ignore units in the headings
Read only the table caption
Read the row and column labels before comparing values

questions.question: Which feature gives a brief overview of a book's chapters and where they begin?
choices: Table of contents
Glossary
Index
Footnote

questions.question: A footnote provides a source for a claim. What does it allow a reader to do?
choices: Determine the text's reading level
Check or explore the supporting reference
Locate a photograph
Identify the plot

questions.question: A diagram labels the parts of a cell. Which question can it answer most directly?
choices: How every cell behaves in every condition
Who discovered all cell structures
Where the labeled structures are positioned relative to one another
Why one organelle is more important

questions.question: A chart uses percentages but does not state the sample size. What limitation should a reader notice?
choices: The chart must be inaccurate
Percentages cannot be used in charts
The topic has no main idea
The percentages alone may hide how many observations they represent

questions.question: How do subheadings help readers?
choices: They divide information into smaller sections with related ideas
They prove each section has equal importance
They replace transitions between ideas
They identify all unfamiliar vocabulary

questions.question: A timeline places events in chronological order. Which relationship does it make easiest to inspect?
choices: Which event caused every other event
When events occurred relative to one another
How reliable each source is
Whether all events have equal importance

questions.question: A photograph is labeled 'before restoration.' What should a reader look for in a related after image?
choices: The author's intended grade level
The publication's table of contents
Changes that can be compared using the same visible features
Words that rhyme in the caption

questions.question: A glossary differs from an index because a glossary
choices: lists chapters, while an index lists authors
shows maps, while an index gives captions
summarizes arguments, while an index gives conclusions
defines selected terms, while an index points to where topics appear

questions.question: An infographic combines icons, short text, and statistics. What should a careful reader do?
choices: Check what each visual represents and where the statistics came from
Assume the design makes every claim factual
Read only the largest number
Ignore the labels because icons are self-explanatory

questions.question: A scale bar appears on a map. What can it help a reader estimate?
choices: The population of each region
Real-world distance represented by a map measurement
The mapmaker's purpose
The age of the map

questions.question: A numbered list presents steps in a process. What does the numbering most likely indicate?
choices: A ranking by reliability
A set of unrelated examples
An intended sequence or order
The amount of evidence for each step

questions.question: Which source feature would best help determine who published an article and when?
choices: A decorative border
A chapter heading
A map scale
Publication information or a byline/date
